The Board of Directors also does not discuss any ratings at its meetings. 1 crore = 10 million Refer to Annexure for Details of Instruments & Bank Facilities Detailed Rationale Crisil Ratings has assigned its 'Crisil A+/Stable' rating to the Rs 6,000 crore non convertible debentures (NCDs) and 'Crisil A1' rating to the short-term bank facilities of GMR Airports Limited (GAL). The ratings reflect strengthening of the business risk profile of GAL, following the expected commencement of duty-free operations at Delhi International Airport Ltd. (DIAL; rated 'Crisil AA-/Stable') and GMR Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (GHIAL; rated 'Crisil AA+/Stable') in July 2025 and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. GAL already operates the duty-free business, car parking, and cargo handling for GMR Goa International Airport Ltd (GGIAL, rated 'Crisil PPMLD A-/Negative') and car parking and retail concessions at GHIAL. Additionally, GAL has signed a concession agreement to operate duty-free, car parking, cargo, and retail concessions at GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Ltd (GVIAL) at Bhogapuram, which is likely to commence operations before December 2026. These are long-term concessions concurrent with the tenure of the airport concession itself. Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards. They will provide steady cash flow to GAL over a longer, given their monopolistic positions as exclusive operators in their respective airports, long term contracts for running these non-aero businesses, alongside a favourable outlook for air passenger traffic at these airports. GAL also has a proven track record of successfully operating these businesses through joint ventures (JVs). The ratings also factor in benefits available to GAL through its strategic co-promoter - Groupe ADP, healthy financial flexibility derived from being a listed holding company of two major operating Indian airports, DIAL and GHIAL, and demonstrated track record of having raised funds in the past to meet refinancing or capital expenditure (capex) requirement. The ratings remain constrained by elevated debt levels, exposure to refinancing risk in view of bullet repayments, and project risk associated with greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram, Crete (Greece) and the brownfield expansion at Nagpur. Analytical Approach Crisil Ratings has evaluated GAL on a standalone basis, factoring in support and equity commitments towards its subsidiaries/special-purpose vehicles (SPVs). Foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs) worth Rs 2,396 crore and optionally convertible and redeemable preference shares (OCRPS) worth Rs 260.4 crore to Groupe ADP, have been treated as neither debt nor equity. Key Rating Drivers & Detailed Description Strengths: Significant improvement in cash flow driven by non-aero business, aided by strategic location, exclusivity agreements, and long-term concessions, positive passenger growth outlook and seasoned management: GAL will benefit from its experienced management, favourable locations that it operates in, the exclusivity agreement and long concession period, along with a positive outlook on passenger traffic growth. Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards. Growth will be driven by commencement of duty-free operations at DIAL and GHIAL in July and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. In fiscal 2025, the Delhi duty free and Hyderabad duty free clocked a revenue of Rs 2,200 crore and Rs 372 crore, respectively. GAL will now operate these concessions on sole basis. Demand-related risk is low, given the monopolistic nature of businesses and GAL's sole operator status at these airports, which would ensure stable cash flow for the long term. Expansion of retail and commercial facilities, enhanced passenger amenities, and improvement in overall airport experience, should aid in increasing the average non- aero spend per passenger. Hence, growth in passenger traffic and non-aero revenue per passenger will boost the operating revenue for GAL. Steady dividends from GHIAL and DIAL (expected in medium term), should further boost operating performance. Extensive experience of GAL's strategic co-promoter, Groupe ADP: Currently, the GMR group holds 33.8% equity stake in GAL, while Groupe ADP holds a 32.3% equity stake, with both entities having an equal board representation. Groupe ADP also has representation on the board of directors of all operational airports and key subsidiaries. As per the agreement between GMR and Groupe ADP, the GMR group will retain management control over GAL, provided it maintains a minimum 10% stake in the company. As a co-promoter, Groupe ADP plays an active role in shaping GAL's strategic and financial decisions, exercising oversight. Groupe ADP manages 26 airports worldwide, including three international airports in Paris. It is majority-owned by the Government of France with a 50.6% stake. Financial flexibility derived from direct ownership of airport assets: GAL, the parent company of DIAL and GHIAL, two major airports, benefits from their robust business risk profiles. Revenue streams at these airports are secured through a hybrid tariff system, guaranteeing returns on aero assets. Passenger traffic at these airports, which accounted for about 30% of total air traffic in fiscal 2025, is likely to grow further. DIAL may also see its financial performance improve from fiscal 2026, driven by a significant tariff hike, pertaining to the completed capex. With this, dividends from DIAL are likely to flow in medium term. Post capex completion, GHIAL is also seeing growth in passenger traffic and revenue and is well-positioned to maintain this momentum. Steady dividends are expected to be accrued from GHIAL. Performance of GGIAL was impacted by subdued passenger traffic growth in Goa in fiscal 2025. Going forward, the airport's ability to ramp up passenger traffic and execute its real estate monetisation plans within the proposed timeline will remain a key monitorable. Proven track record for fund-raising: GAL raised Rs 5,000 crore via non-convertible bonds in the third and fourth quarter of fiscal 2024, prior to its merger with the erstwhile GMR Airport Infrastructure Ltd, to finance its existing debt, buy out 11% stake held by Malaysia Airports Holdings Berhad (MAHB) in GHIAL, and to maintain additional liquidity for equity investments in new projects. GAL has a proven history of securing funds to meet its refinancing and capex needs for its airport assets. Although successful fundraising has enabled the company to meet its refinancing requirement, high cost of debt had exerted pressure on cash flow earlier. Nevertheless, in recent years, the company has seen its cost of debt decline, which should have a positive impact on its financial performance. De-linking from GPUIL with no further recourse to GAL: As on date, GAL has no corporate guarantees or contingent liabilities related to GMR Power & Urban Infra Ltd (GPUIL). The management has articulated that GAL will not extend any corporate guarantees or loans to any non-airport related business in future. That said, GAL has extended around Rs 2200 crore via inter-corporate deposits (ICDs; excluding around Rs 600 crore of accrued interest) to GPUIL and its subsidiaries. As per the management, GPUIL is expected to repay the ICDs between fiscals 2026 and 2029, which in turn will reduce GAL's debt and strengthen its financial position. Weaknesses: Elevated debt levels & refinancing risk: The company reported an elevated net debt (excluding FCCBs and accrued interest) to Ebitda (including dividends) ratio of 9.5 times as on March 31, 2025. As articulated by the management, the ratio is expected to decrease significantly over the next 3-4 years, driven by healthy cash accrual, which will be retained to reduce debt. Extent of deleveraging remains a key monitorable. The management has stated that GAL will start making dividend payments to its shareholders once it achieves its debt reduction target. Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) should remain comfortable over the medium term, supported by bullet payments and accumulated interest components of debt. Furthermore, the company's strong track record in refinancing and healthy valuations of its underlying assets will mitigate refinancing risk and offer some degree of comfort to manage the debt obligations. The GMR group intends to buy and convert FCCBs worth Rs 2,396 crore issued to Groupe ADP, over a period of time, without imposing any additional financial liability on GAL.GAL held NCBs worth Rs 6,100 crore as on March 31, 2025. Of these, bonds worth Rs 5,000 crore have a bullet repayment in November 2026, while bonds worth Rs 1,100 crore have a bullet repayment in February 2028. In addition, GAL had raised Rs 400 crore via NCBs in April 2025, which have a bullet repayment in April 2028. This exposes the company to significant refinancing risk. However, a strong track record of timely refinancing mitigates this risk to an extent. Pledge of shares in GAL by the promoters, albeit decreasing, remains high: As of March 21, 2025, the promoters have pledged 35% of the GMR group's stake in GAL (down from 54% as of July 25, 2024) to secure debt at the promoter entity level. Any increase in pledged shares will be a key monitorable. Susceptibility to project risk arising from greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram and Crete and brownfield expansion at Nagpur: With greenfield airports at Bhogapuram, Andhra Pradesh and Crete, Greece under implementation, GAL remains exposed to project risk. Furthermore, the Airports Authority of India ('Crisil AAA/Stable') has earmarked 11 airports to be privatised in fiscal 2026. Winning the bid to operate, manage and develop any of these airports will also expose GAL to project related risk. Crisil Ratings has factored in equity support/investment of Rs 300-400 crore per annum towards these projects in the medium term. Any material increase in equity support will be a key sensitivity factor. Liquidity: Adequate The company had cash and cash equivalents of around Rs 340 crore against total debt of Rs 6,248 crore (excluding FCCBs and accrued interest) as on March 31, 2025. While the company had an interest obligation of Rs 962 crore in fiscal 2025, it resorted to cash coupon payments of Rs 387 crore for servicing its interest and balance through the accumulated interest. It has fulfilled its entire equity commitment in its operating airport projects, held via subsidiaries and JVs. The company is likely to infuse Rs 113 crore towards the Bhogapuram airport in fiscal 2026, of which Rs 51 crore has been infused till date. Environment, social and governance (ESG) profile Crisil Ratings believes the ESG profile of GAL supports its strong credit risk profile. · In line with the Airport Council International's (ACI) Airport Carbon Accreditation (ACA) programme, DIAL and GHIAL has successfully achieved Level 5 requirements, which is the highest-level accreditation of the programme. This makes GMR Airports the largest airport group globally to manage and operate Level 5 accredited airports. The airport at Mopa, in Goa, targets carbon neutrality and achieving ACI Level 3+ by 2027. · In 2024, airports under GAL increased its renewable energy consumption by 42% (year-on-year), with renewable energy accounting for 89% of its overall energy mix. This led to reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions intensity by nearly 72% (y-o-y) to 2.5 tCO2e per Rs crore of revenue reported. Both Delhi and Hyderabad airports operate on clean electricity, reflecting GAL's focus and commitment towards net zero emissions. This is achieved through a combination of onsite solar units and clean power agreements. . In fiscal 2024, women formed nearly 13% of total employees and the overall attrition was ~12%, at the consolidated level. · The governance structure is characterised by 50% of independent directors, ~6% women directors, a fully independent audit committee, largely independent risk management and nomination and remuneration committees, and extensive financial disclosures. The Board also has an ESG Committee which takes stock of ESG Progress on regular basis. Outlook: Stable Crisil Ratings believes GAL's business risk profile should strengthen, with the commencement of stable non-aeronautical revenue streams. The financial risk profile will improve, characterised by healthy cash accrual and deleveraging. Rating sensitivity factors Upward factors · Significant reduction in debt, leading to net debt/Ebitda (including dividends) of 5.5-6 times on a sustained basis, coupled with adequate debt servicing ability · Timely and healthy scale up of non-aero businesses, along with sustenance of a healthy operating margin Downward factors · Delayed correction in debt or lower-than-expected cash accrual from non-aero businesses, leading to net debt/ adjusted Ebitda of 9-9.5 times on a sustained basis · Depletion of liquidity, considering cash outflow via dividends, loans and advances, equity support to subsidiaries / SPVs resulting in stretched liquidity About the Company GAL is a leading airport developer and operator in India, with a portfolio of airports, including DIAL, GHIAL, GGIAL and Medan International Airport, as well as upcoming projects such as Bhogapuram International Airport and Crete International Airport (Greece), catering to millions of passengers annually. The company also recently signed the concession agreement for Babasaheb International Airports, Nagpur, further expanding its footprint in the country. The company has been promoted by the GMR Group, with a shareholding structure that includes Groupe ADP (32.3%), GMR group 33.8%), and other investors, showcasing a strong partnership between Indian and international stakeholders. About the Group The GMR group is a global infrastructure conglomerate with a diverse portfolio of businesses, including airports, energy, transportation, and urban infrastructure, operating in India, Asia, and Europe. Established in 1978, the group's business interests span multiple sectors, with a focus on infrastructure development and operations. paragraphs.content: GMR Airports Limited 'Crisil A+/Stable' assigned to Non Convertible Debentures; 'Crisil A1' assigned to Bank Debt

Note: None of the Directors on Crisil Ratings Limited's Board are members of rating committee and thus do not participate in discussion or assignment of any ratings. The Board of Directors also does not discuss any ratings at its meetings.
Refer to Annexure for Details of Instruments & Bank Facilities

Crisil Ratings has assigned its 'Crisil A+/Stable' rating to the Rs 6,000 crore non convertible debentures (NCDs) and 'Crisil A1' rating to the short-term bank facilities of GMR Airports Limited (GAL).

The ratings reflect strengthening of the business risk profile of GAL, following the expected commencement of duty-free operations at Delhi International Airport Ltd. (DIAL; rated 'Crisil AA-/Stable') and GMR Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (GHIAL; rated 'Crisil AA+/Stable') in July 2025 and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. GAL already operates the duty-free business, car parking, and cargo handling for GMR Goa International Airport Ltd (GGIAL, rated 'Crisil PPMLD A-/Negative') and car parking and retail concessions at GHIAL. Additionally, GAL has signed a concession agreement to operate duty-free, car parking, cargo, and retail concessions at GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Ltd (GVIAL) at Bhogapuram, which is likely to commence operations before December 2026. These are long-term concessions concurrent with the tenure of the airport concession itself.

Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards. They will provide steady cash flow to GAL over a longer, given their monopolistic positions as exclusive operators in their respective airports, long term contracts for running these non-aero businesses, alongside a favourable outlook for air passenger traffic at these airports. GAL also has a proven track record of successfully operating these businesses through joint ventures (JVs).

The ratings also factor in benefits available to GAL through its strategic co-promoter - Groupe ADP, healthy financial flexibility derived from being a listed holding company of two major operating Indian airports, DIAL and GHIAL, and demonstrated track record of having raised funds in the past to meet refinancing or capital expenditure (capex) requirement.

The ratings remain constrained by elevated debt levels, exposure to refinancing risk in view of bullet repayments, and project risk associated with greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram, Crete (Greece) and the brownfield expansion at Nagpur.
Crisil Ratings has evaluated GAL on a standalone basis, factoring in support and equity commitments towards its subsidiaries/special-purpose vehicles (SPVs).

Foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs) worth Rs 2,396 crore and optionally convertible and redeemable preference shares (OCRPS) worth Rs 260.4 crore to Groupe ADP, have been treated as neither debt nor equity.

Significant improvement in cash flow driven by non-aero business, aided by strategic location, exclusivity agreements, and long-term concessions, positive passenger growth outlook and seasoned management: GAL will benefit from its experienced management, favourable locations that it operates in, the exclusivity agreement and long concession period, along with a positive outlook on passenger traffic growth.
Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards.

Growth will be driven by commencement of duty-free operations at DIAL and GHIAL in July and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. In fiscal 2025, the Delhi duty free and Hyderabad duty free clocked a revenue of Rs 2,200 crore and Rs 372 crore, respectively. GAL will now operate these concessions on sole basis. Demand-related risk is low, given the monopolistic nature of businesses and GAL's sole operator status at these airports, which would ensure stable cash flow for the long term. Expansion of retail and commercial facilities, enhanced passenger amenities, and improvement in overall airport experience, should aid in increasing the average non- aero spend per passenger. Hence, growth in passenger traffic and non-aero revenue per passenger will boost the operating revenue for GAL.
Steady dividends from GHIAL and DIAL (expected in medium term), should further boost operating performance.

Extensive experience of GAL's strategic co-promoter, Groupe ADP: Currently, the GMR group holds 33.8% equity stake in GAL, while Groupe ADP holds a 32.3% equity stake, with both entities having an equal board representation. Groupe ADP also has representation on the board of directors of all operational airports and key subsidiaries.

As per the agreement between GMR and Groupe ADP, the GMR group will retain management control over GAL, provided it maintains a minimum 10% stake in the company. As a co-promoter, Groupe ADP plays an active role in shaping GAL's strategic and financial decisions, exercising oversight.
Groupe ADP manages 26 airports worldwide, including three international airports in Paris. It is majority-owned by the Government of France with a 50.6% stake.

Financial flexibility derived from direct ownership of airport assets: GAL, the parent company of DIAL and GHIAL, two major airports, benefits from their robust business risk profiles. Revenue streams at these airports are secured through a hybrid tariff system, guaranteeing returns on aero assets. Passenger traffic at these airports, which accounted for about 30% of total air traffic in fiscal 2025, is likely to grow further. DIAL may also see its financial performance improve from fiscal 2026, driven by a significant tariff hike, pertaining to the completed capex. With this, dividends from DIAL are likely to flow in medium term. Post capex completion, GHIAL is also seeing growth in passenger traffic and revenue and is well-positioned to maintain this momentum. Steady dividends are expected to be accrued from GHIAL.

Performance of GGIAL was impacted by subdued passenger traffic growth in Goa in fiscal 2025. Going forward, the airport's ability to ramp up passenger traffic and execute its real estate monetisation plans within the proposed timeline will remain a key monitorable.

Proven track record for fund-raising: GAL raised Rs 5,000 crore via non-convertible bonds in the third and fourth quarter of fiscal 2024, prior to its merger with the erstwhile GMR Airport Infrastructure Ltd, to finance its existing debt, buy out 11% stake held by Malaysia Airports Holdings Berhad (MAHB) in GHIAL, and to maintain additional liquidity for equity investments in new projects. GAL has a proven history of securing funds to meet its refinancing and capex needs for its airport assets. Although successful fundraising has enabled the company to meet its refinancing requirement, high cost of debt had exerted pressure on cash flow earlier. Nevertheless, in recent years, the company has seen its cost of debt decline, which should have a positive impact on its financial performance.

De-linking from GPUIL with no further recourse to GAL: As on date, GAL has no corporate guarantees or contingent liabilities related to GMR Power & Urban Infra Ltd (GPUIL). The management has articulated that GAL will not extend any corporate guarantees or loans to any non-airport related business in future. That said, GAL has extended around Rs 2200 crore via inter-corporate deposits (ICDs; excluding around Rs 600 crore of accrued interest) to GPUIL and its subsidiaries. As per the management, GPUIL is expected to repay the ICDs between fiscals 2026 and 2029, which in turn will reduce GAL's debt and strengthen its financial position.

Elevated debt levels & refinancing risk: The company reported an elevated net debt (excluding FCCBs and accrued interest) to Ebitda (including dividends) ratio of 9.5 times as on March 31, 2025. As articulated by the management, the ratio is expected to decrease significantly over the next 3-4 years, driven by healthy cash accrual, which will be retained to reduce debt. Extent of deleveraging remains a key monitorable. The management has stated that GAL will start making dividend payments to its shareholders once it achieves its debt reduction target.

Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) should remain comfortable over the medium term, supported by bullet payments and accumulated interest components of debt. Furthermore, the company's strong track record in refinancing and healthy valuations of its underlying assets will mitigate refinancing risk and offer some degree of comfort to manage the debt obligations.

The GMR group intends to buy and convert FCCBs worth Rs 2,396 crore issued to Groupe ADP, over a period of time, without imposing any additional financial liability on GAL.GAL held NCBs worth Rs 6,100 crore as on March 31, 2025. Of these, bonds worth Rs 5,000 crore have a bullet repayment in November 2026, while bonds worth Rs 1,100 crore have a bullet repayment in February 2028. In addition, GAL had raised Rs 400 crore via NCBs in April 2025, which have a bullet
repayment in April 2028. This exposes the company to significant refinancing risk. However, a strong track record of timely refinancing mitigates this risk to an extent.

Pledge of shares in GAL by the promoters, albeit decreasing, remains high: As of March 21, 2025, the promoters have pledged 35% of the GMR group's stake in GAL (down from 54% as of July 25, 2024) to secure debt at the promoter entity level. Any increase in pledged shares will be a key monitorable.
Susceptibility to project risk arising from greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram and Crete and brownfield expansion

at Nagpur: With greenfield airports at Bhogapuram, Andhra Pradesh and Crete, Greece under implementation, GAL remains exposed to project risk. Furthermore, the Airports Authority of India ('Crisil AAA/Stable') has earmarked 11 airports to be privatised in fiscal 2026. Winning the bid to operate, manage and develop any of these airports will also expose GAL to project related risk. Crisil Ratings has factored in equity support/investment of Rs 300-400 crore per annum towards these projects in the medium term. Any material increase in equity support will be a key sensitivity factor.

The company had cash and cash equivalents of around Rs 340 crore against total debt of Rs 6,248 crore (excluding FCCBs and accrued interest) as on March 31, 2025. While the company had an interest obligation of Rs 962 crore in fiscal 2025, it resorted to cash coupon payments of Rs 387 crore for servicing its interest and balance through the accumulated interest. It has fulfilled its entire equity commitment in its operating airport projects, held via subsidiaries and JVs. The company is likely to infuse Rs 113 crore towards the Bhogapuram airport in fiscal 2026, of which Rs 51 crore has been infused till date.
Crisil Ratings believes the ESG profile of GAL supports its strong credit risk profile.

· In line with the Airport Council International's (ACI) Airport Carbon Accreditation (ACA) programme, DIAL and GHIAL has successfully achieved Level 5 requirements, which is the highest-level accreditation of the programme. This makes GMR Airports the largest airport group globally to manage and operate Level 5 accredited airports. The airport at Mopa, in Goa, targets carbon neutrality and achieving ACI Level 3+ by 2027.

· In 2024, airports under GAL increased its renewable energy consumption by 42% (year-on-year), with renewable energy accounting for 89% of its overall energy mix. This led to reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions intensity by nearly 72% (y-o-y) to 2.5 tCO2e per Rs crore of revenue reported. Both Delhi and Hyderabad airports operate on clean electricity, reflecting GAL's focus and commitment towards net zero emissions. This is achieved through a combination of onsite solar units and clean power agreements.
. In fiscal 2024, women formed nearly 13% of total employees and the overall attrition was ~12%, at the consolidated level.

· The governance structure is characterised by 50% of independent directors, ~6% women directors, a fully independent audit committee, largely independent risk management and nomination and remuneration committees, and extensive financial disclosures. The Board also has an ESG Committee which takes stock of ESG Progress on regular basis.

Crisil Ratings believes GAL's business risk profile should strengthen, with the commencement of stable non-aeronautical revenue streams. The financial risk profile will improve, characterised by healthy cash accrual and deleveraging.
· Significant reduction in debt, leading to net debt/Ebitda (including dividends) of 5.5-6 times on a sustained basis, coupled with adequate debt servicing ability
· Timely and healthy scale up of non-aero businesses, along with sustenance of a healthy operating margin
· Delayed correction in debt or lower-than-expected cash accrual from non-aero businesses, leading to net debt/ adjusted Ebitda of 9-9.5 times on a sustained basis
· Depletion of liquidity, considering cash outflow via dividends, loans and advances, equity support to subsidiaries / SPVs resulting in stretched liquidity

GAL is a leading airport developer and operator in India, with a portfolio of airports, including DIAL, GHIAL, GGIAL and Medan International Airport, as well as upcoming projects such as Bhogapuram International Airport and Crete International Airport (Greece), catering to millions of passengers annually. The company also recently signed the concession agreement for Babasaheb International Airports, Nagpur, further expanding its footprint in the country. The company has been promoted by the GMR Group, with a shareholding structure that includes Groupe ADP (32.3%), GMR group 33.8%), and other investors, showcasing a strong partnership between Indian and international stakeholders.

The GMR group is a global infrastructure conglomerate with a diverse portfolio of businesses, including airports, energy, transportation, and urban infrastructure, operating in India, Asia, and Europe. Established in 1978, the group's business interests span multiple sectors, with a focus on infrastructure development and operations.

<<P:1:19>> Crisil Ratings has assigned its 'Crisil A+/Stable' rating to the Rs 6,000 crore non convertible debentures (NCDs) and 'Crisil
<<P:1:20>> A1' rating to the short-term bank facilities of GMR Airports Limited (GAL).
<<P:1:21>> The ratings reflect strengthening of the business risk profile of GAL, following the expected commencement of duty-free
<<P:1:22>> operations at Delhi International Airport Ltd. (DIAL; rated 'Crisil AA-/Stable') and GMR Hyderabad International Airport Ltd.
<<P:1:23>> (GHIAL; rated 'Crisil AA+/Stable') in July 2025 and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30
<<P:1:24>> years) and 20 years, respectively. GAL already operates the duty-free business, car parking, and cargo handling for GMR
<<P:1:25>> Goa International Airport Ltd (GGIAL, rated 'Crisil PPMLD A-/Negative') and car parking and retail concessions at GHIAL.
<<P:1:26>> Additionally, GAL has signed a concession agreement to operate duty-free, car parking, cargo, and retail concessions at
<<P:1:27>> GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Ltd (GVIAL) at Bhogapuram, which is likely to commence operations before
<<P:1:28>> December 2026. These are long-term concessions concurrent with the tenure of the airport concession itself.
<<P:1:29>> Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards. They will provide
<<P:1:30>> steady cash flow to GAL over a longer, given their monopolistic positions as exclusive operators in their respective airports,
<<P:1:31>> long term contracts for running these non-aero businesses, alongside a favourable outlook for air passenger traffic at these
<<P:1:32>> airports. GAL also has a proven track record of successfully operating these businesses through joint ventures (JVs).
<<P:1:33>> The ratings also factor in benefits available to GAL through its strategic co-promoter - Groupe ADP, healthy financial
<<P:1:34>> flexibility derived from being a listed holding company of two major operating Indian airports, DIAL and GHIAL, and
<<P:1:35>> demonstrated track record of having raised funds in the past to meet refinancing or capital expenditure (capex) requirement.
<<P:1:36>> The ratings remain constrained by elevated debt levels, exposure to refinancing risk in view of bullet repayments, and
<<P:1:37>> project risk associated with greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram, Crete (Greece) and the brownfield expansion at Nagpur.
<<P:1:38>> Analytical Approach
<<P:1:39>> Crisil Ratings has evaluated GAL on a standalone basis, factoring in support and equity commitments towards its
<<P:1:40>> subsidiaries/special-purpose vehicles (SPVs).
<<P:1:41>> Foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs) worth Rs 2,396 crore and optionally convertible and redeemable preference
<<P:1:42>> shares (OCRPS) worth Rs 260.4 crore to Groupe ADP, have been treated as neither debt nor equity.

<<P:1:44>> Strengths:
<<P:1:45>> Significant improvement in cash flow driven by non-aero business, aided by strategic location, exclusivity
<<P:1:46>> agreements, and long-term concessions, positive passenger growth outlook and seasoned management: GAL will
<<P:1:47>> benefit from its experienced management, favourable locations that it operates in, the exclusivity agreement and long
<<P:1:48>> concession period, along with a positive outlook on passenger traffic growth.
<<P:1:49>> Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards.
<<PAGE:2>>
<<P:2:1>> Growth will be driven by commencement of duty-free operations at DIAL and GHIAL in July and August 2025, respectively,
<<P:2:2>> for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. In fiscal 2025, the Delhi duty free and
<<P:2:3>> Hyderabad duty free clocked a revenue of Rs 2,200 crore and Rs 372 crore, respectively. GAL will now operate these
<<P:2:4>> concessions on sole basis. Demand-related risk is low, given the monopolistic nature of businesses and GAL's sole operator
<<P:2:5>> status at these airports, which would ensure stable cash flow for the long term. Expansion of retail and commercial facilities,
<<P:2:6>> enhanced passenger amenities, and improvement in overall airport experience, should aid in increasing the average non-
<<P:2:7>> aero spend per passenger. Hence, growth in passenger traffic and non-aero revenue per passenger will boost the operating
<<P:2:8>> revenue for GAL.
<<P:2:9>> Steady dividends from GHIAL and DIAL (expected in medium term), should further boost operating performance.
<<P:2:10>> Extensive experience of GAL's strategic co-promoter, Groupe ADP: Currently, the GMR group holds 33.8% equity
<<P:2:11>> stake in GAL, while Groupe ADP holds a 32.3% equity stake, with both entities having an equal board representation.
<<P:2:12>> Groupe ADP also has representation on the board of directors of all operational airports and key subsidiaries.
<<P:2:13>> As per the agreement between GMR and Groupe ADP, the GMR group will retain management control over GAL, provided it
<<P:2:14>> maintains a minimum 10% stake in the company. As a co-promoter, Groupe ADP plays an active role in shaping GAL's
<<P:2:15>> strategic and financial decisions, exercising oversight.
<<P:2:16>> Groupe ADP manages 26 airports worldwide, including three international airports in Paris. It is majority-owned by the
<<P:2:17>> Government of France with a 50.6% stake.
<<P:2:18>> Financial flexibility derived from direct ownership of airport assets: GAL, the parent company of DIAL and GHIAL, two
<<P:2:19>> major airports, benefits from their robust business risk profiles. Revenue streams at these airports are secured through a
<<P:2:20>> hybrid tariff system, guaranteeing returns on aero assets. Passenger traffic at these airports, which accounted for about
<<P:2:21>> 30% of total air traffic in fiscal 2025, is likely to grow further. DIAL may also see its financial performance improve from fiscal
<<P:2:22>> 2026, driven by a significant tariff hike, pertaining to the completed capex. With this, dividends from DIAL are likely to flow in
<<P:2:23>> medium term. Post capex completion, GHIAL is also seeing growth in passenger traffic and revenue and is well-positioned
<<P:2:24>> to maintain this momentum. Steady dividends are expected to be accrued from GHIAL.
<<P:2:25>> Performance of GGIAL was impacted by subdued passenger traffic growth in Goa in fiscal 2025. Going forward, the airport's
<<P:2:26>> ability to ramp up passenger traffic and execute its real estate monetisation plans within the proposed timeline will remain a
<<P:2:27>> key monitorable.
<<P:2:28>> Proven track record for fund-raising: GAL raised Rs 5,000 crore via non-convertible bonds in the third and fourth quarter
<<P:2:29>> of fiscal 2024, prior to its merger with the erstwhile GMR Airport Infrastructure Ltd, to finance its existing debt, buy out 11%
<<P:2:30>> stake held by Malaysia Airports Holdings Berhad (MAHB) in GHIAL, and to maintain additional liquidity for equity
<<P:2:31>> investments in new projects. GAL has a proven history of securing funds to meet its refinancing and capex needs for its
<<P:2:32>> airport assets. Although successful fundraising has enabled the company to meet its refinancing requirement, high cost of
<<P:2:33>> debt had exerted pressure on cash flow earlier. Nevertheless, in recent years, the company has seen its cost of debt
<<P:2:34>> decline, which should have a positive impact on its financial performance.
<<P:2:35>> De-linking from GPUIL with no further recourse to GAL: As on date, GAL has no corporate guarantees or contingent
<<P:2:36>> liabilities related to GMR Power & Urban Infra Ltd (GPUIL). The management has articulated that GAL will not extend any
<<P:2:37>> corporate guarantees or loans to any non-airport related business in future. That said, GAL has extended around Rs 2200
<<P:2:38>> crore via inter-corporate deposits (ICDs; excluding around Rs 600 crore of accrued interest) to GPUIL and its subsidiaries.
<<P:2:39>> As per the management, GPUIL is expected to repay the ICDs between fiscals 2026 and 2029, which in turn will reduce
<<P:2:40>> GAL's debt and strengthen its financial position.
<<P:2:41>> Weaknesses:
<<P:2:42>> Elevated debt levels & refinancing risk: The company reported an elevated net debt (excluding FCCBs and accrued
<<P:2:43>> interest) to Ebitda (including dividends) ratio of 9.5 times as on March 31, 2025. As articulated by the management, the ratio
<<P:2:44>> is expected to decrease significantly over the next 3-4 years, driven by healthy cash accrual, which will be retained to
<<P:2:45>> reduce debt. Extent of deleveraging remains a key monitorable. The management has stated that GAL will start making
<<P:2:46>> dividend payments to its shareholders once it achieves its debt reduction target.
<<P:2:47>> Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) should remain comfortable over the medium term, supported by bullet payments and
<<P:2:48>> accumulated interest components of debt. Furthermore, the company's strong track record in refinancing and healthy
<<P:2:49>> valuations of its underlying assets will mitigate refinancing risk and offer some degree of comfort to manage the debt
<<P:2:50>> obligations.
<<P:2:51>> The GMR group intends to buy and convert FCCBs worth Rs 2,396 crore issued to Groupe ADP, over a period of time,
<<P:2:52>> without imposing any additional financial liability on GAL.GAL held NCBs worth Rs 6,100 crore as on March 31, 2025. Of
<<P:2:53>> these, bonds worth Rs 5,000 crore have a bullet repayment in November 2026, while bonds worth Rs 1,100 crore have a
<<P:2:54>> bullet repayment in February 2028. In addition, GAL had raised Rs 400 crore via NCBs in April 2025, which have a bullet
<<PAGE:3>>
<<P:3:1>> repayment in April 2028. This exposes the company to significant refinancing risk. However, a strong track record of timely
<<P:3:2>> refinancing mitigates this risk to an extent.
<<P:3:3>> Pledge of shares in GAL by the promoters, albeit decreasing, remains high: As of March 21, 2025, the promoters have
<<P:3:4>> pledged 35% of the GMR group's stake in GAL (down from 54% as of July 25, 2024) to secure debt at the promoter entity
<<P:3:5>> level. Any increase in pledged shares will be a key monitorable.
<<P:3:6>> Susceptibility to project risk arising from greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram and Crete and brownfield expansion
<<P:3:7>> at Nagpur: With greenfield airports at Bhogapuram, Andhra Pradesh and Crete, Greece under implementation, GAL
<<P:3:8>> remains exposed to project risk. Furthermore, the Airports Authority of India ('Crisil AAA/Stable') has earmarked 11 airports
<<P:3:9>> to be privatised in fiscal 2026. Winning the bid to operate, manage and develop any of these airports will also expose GAL
<<P:3:10>> to project related risk. Crisil Ratings has factored in equity support/investment of Rs 300-400 crore per annum towards
<<P:3:11>> these projects in the medium term. Any material increase in equity support will be a key sensitivity factor.

<<P:3:14>> and accrued interest) as on March 31, 2025. While the company had an interest obligation of Rs 962 crore in fiscal 2025, it
<<P:3:15>> resorted to cash coupon payments of Rs 387 crore for servicing its interest and balance through the accumulated interest. It
<<P:3:16>> has fulfilled its entire equity commitment in its operating airport projects, held via subsidiaries and JVs. The company is
<<P:3:17>> likely to infuse Rs 113 crore towards the Bhogapuram airport in fiscal 2026, of which Rs 51 crore has been infused till date.
<<P:3:18>> Environment, social and governance (ESG) profile
<<P:3:19>> Crisil Ratings believes the ESG profile of GAL supports its strong credit risk profile.
<<P:3:20>> · In line with the Airport Council International's (ACI) Airport Carbon Accreditation (ACA) programme, DIAL and GHIAL
<<P:3:21>> has successfully achieved Level 5 requirements, which is the highest-level accreditation of the programme. This makes
<<P:3:22>> GMR Airports the largest airport group globally to manage and operate Level 5 accredited airports. The airport at Mopa,
<<P:3:23>> in Goa, targets carbon neutrality and achieving ACI Level 3+ by 2027.
<<P:3:24>> · In 2024, airports under GAL increased its renewable energy consumption by 42% (year-on-year), with renewable
<<P:3:25>> energy accounting for 89% of its overall energy mix. This led to reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions intensity by nearly
<<P:3:26>> 72% (y-o-y) to 2.5 tCO2e per Rs crore of revenue reported. Both Delhi and Hyderabad airports operate on clean
<<P:3:27>> electricity, reflecting GAL's focus and commitment towards net zero emissions. This is achieved through a combination
<<P:3:28>> of onsite solar units and clean power agreements.
<<P:3:29>> . In fiscal 2024, women formed nearly 13% of total employees and the overall attrition was ~12%, at the consolidated
<<P:3:30>> level.
<<P:3:31>> · The governance structure is characterised by 50% of independent directors, ~6% women directors, a fully independent
<<P:3:32>> audit committee, largely independent risk management and nomination and remuneration committees, and extensive
<<P:3:33>> financial disclosures. The Board also has an ESG Committee which takes stock of ESG Progress on regular basis.

<<PARA:1:14>> Detailed Rationale
<<PARA:1:15>> Crisil Ratings has assigned its 'Crisil A+/Stable' rating to the Rs 6,000 crore non convertible debentures (NCDs) and 'Crisil A1' rating to the short-term bank facilities of GMR Airports Limited (GAL).
<<PARA:1:16>> The ratings reflect strengthening of the business risk profile of GAL, following the expected commencement of duty-free operations at Delhi International Airport Ltd. (DIAL; rated 'Crisil AA-/Stable') and GMR Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (GHIAL; rated 'Crisil AA+/Stable') in July 2025 and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. GAL already operates the duty-free business, car parking, and cargo handling for GMR Goa International Airport Ltd (GGIAL, rated 'Crisil PPMLD A-/Negative') and car parking and retail concessions at GHIAL. Additionally, GAL has signed a concession agreement to operate duty-free, car parking, cargo, and retail concessions at GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Ltd (GVIAL) at Bhogapuram, which is likely to commence operations before December 2026. These are long-term concessions concurrent with the tenure of the airport concession itself.
<<PARA:1:17>> Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards. They will provide steady cash flow to GAL over a longer, given their monopolistic positions as exclusive operators in their respective airports, long term contracts for running these non-aero businesses, alongside a favourable outlook for air passenger traffic at these airports. GAL also has a proven track record of successfully operating these businesses through joint ventures (JVs).
<<PARA:1:18>> The ratings also factor in benefits available to GAL through its strategic co-promoter - Groupe ADP, healthy financial flexibility derived from being a listed holding company of two major operating Indian airports, DIAL and GHIAL, and demonstrated track record of having raised funds in the past to meet refinancing or capital expenditure (capex) requirement.
<<PARA:1:19>> The ratings remain constrained by elevated debt levels, exposure to refinancing risk in view of bullet repayments, and project risk associated with greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram, Crete (Greece) and the brownfield expansion at Nagpur.
<<PARA:1:20>> Analytical Approach
<<PARA:1:21>> Crisil Ratings has evaluated GAL on a standalone basis, factoring in support and equity commitments towards its subsidiaries/special-purpose vehicles (SPVs).
<<PARA:1:22>> Foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs) worth Rs 2,396 crore and optionally convertible and redeemable preference shares (OCRPS) worth Rs 260.4 crore to Groupe ADP, have been treated as neither debt nor equity.
<<PARA:1:23>> Key Rating Drivers & Detailed Description
<<PARA:1:24>> Strengths:
<<PARA:1:25>> Significant improvement in cash flow driven by non-aero business, aided by strategic location, exclusivity agreements, and long-term concessions, positive passenger growth outlook and seasoned management: GAL will benefit from its experienced management, favourable locations that it operates in, the exclusivity agreement and long concession period, along with a positive outlook on passenger traffic growth.
<<PARA:1:26>> Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards.
<<PARA:2:27>> Growth will be driven by commencement of duty-free operations at DIAL and GHIAL in July and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. In fiscal 2025, the Delhi duty free and Hyderabad duty free clocked a revenue of Rs 2,200 crore and Rs 372 crore, respectively. GAL will now operate these concessions on sole basis. Demand-related risk is low, given the monopolistic nature of businesses and GAL's sole operator status at these airports, which would ensure stable cash flow for the long term. Expansion of retail and commercial facilities, enhanced passenger amenities, and improvement in overall airport experience, should aid in increasing the average non- aero spend per passenger. Hence, growth in passenger traffic and non-aero revenue per passenger will boost the operating revenue for GAL.
<<PARA:2:28>> Steady dividends from GHIAL and DIAL (expected in medium term), should further boost operating performance.
<<PARA:2:29>> Extensive experience of GAL's strategic co-promoter, Groupe ADP: Currently, the GMR group holds 33.8% equity stake in GAL, while Groupe ADP holds a 32.3% equity stake, with both entities having an equal board representation. Groupe ADP also has representation on the board of directors of all operational airports and key subsidiaries.
<<PARA:2:30>> As per the agreement between GMR and Groupe ADP, the GMR group will retain management control over GAL, provided it maintains a minimum 10% stake in the company. As a co-promoter, Groupe ADP plays an active role in shaping GAL's strategic and financial decisions, exercising oversight.
<<PARA:2:31>> Groupe ADP manages 26 airports worldwide, including three international airports in Paris. It is majority-owned by the Government of France with a 50.6% stake.
<<PARA:2:32>> Financial flexibility derived from direct ownership of airport assets: GAL, the parent company of DIAL and GHIAL, two major airports, benefits from their robust business risk profiles. Revenue streams at these airports are secured through a hybrid tariff system, guaranteeing returns on aero assets. Passenger traffic at these airports, which accounted for about 30% of total air traffic in fiscal 2025, is likely to grow further. DIAL may also see its financial performance improve from fiscal 2026, driven by a significant tariff hike, pertaining to the completed capex. With this, dividends from DIAL are likely to flow in medium term. Post capex completion, GHIAL is also seeing growth in passenger traffic and revenue and is well-positioned to maintain this momentum. Steady dividends are expected to be accrued from GHIAL.
<<PARA:2:33>> Performance of GGIAL was impacted by subdued passenger traffic growth in Goa in fiscal 2025. Going forward, the airport's ability to ramp up passenger traffic and execute its real estate monetisation plans within the proposed timeline will remain a key monitorable.
<<PARA:2:34>> Proven track record for fund-raising: GAL raised Rs 5,000 crore via non-convertible bonds in the third and fourth quarter of fiscal 2024, prior to its merger with the erstwhile GMR Airport Infrastructure Ltd, to finance its existing debt, buy out 11% stake held by Malaysia Airports Holdings Berhad (MAHB) in GHIAL, and to maintain additional liquidity for equity investments in new projects. GAL has a proven history of securing funds to meet its refinancing and capex needs for its airport assets. Although successful fundraising has enabled the company to meet its refinancing requirement, high cost of debt had exerted pressure on cash flow earlier. Nevertheless, in recent years, the company has seen its cost of debt decline, which should have a positive impact on its financial performance.
<<PARA:2:35>> De-linking from GPUIL with no further recourse to GAL: As on date, GAL has no corporate guarantees or contingent liabilities related to GMR Power & Urban Infra Ltd (GPUIL). The management has articulated that GAL will not extend any corporate guarantees or loans to any non-airport related business in future. That said, GAL has extended around Rs 2200 crore via inter-corporate deposits (ICDs; excluding around Rs 600 crore of accrued interest) to GPUIL and its subsidiaries. As per the management, GPUIL is expected to repay the ICDs between fiscals 2026 and 2029, which in turn will reduce GAL's debt and strengthen its financial position.
<<PARA:2:36>> Weaknesses:
<<PARA:2:37>> Elevated debt levels & refinancing risk: The company reported an elevated net debt (excluding FCCBs and accrued interest) to Ebitda (including dividends) ratio of 9.5 times as on March 31, 2025. As articulated by the management, the ratio is expected to decrease significantly over the next 3-4 years, driven by healthy cash accrual, which will be retained to reduce debt. Extent of deleveraging remains a key monitorable. The management has stated that GAL will start making dividend payments to its shareholders once it achieves its debt reduction target.
<<PARA:2:38>> Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) should remain comfortable over the medium term, supported by bullet payments and accumulated interest components of debt. Furthermore, the company's strong track record in refinancing and healthy valuations of its underlying assets will mitigate refinancing risk and offer some degree of comfort to manage the debt obligations.
<<PARA:2:39>> The GMR group intends to buy and convert FCCBs worth Rs 2,396 crore issued to Groupe ADP, over a period of time, without imposing any additional financial liability on GAL.GAL held NCBs worth Rs 6,100 crore as on March 31, 2025. Of these, bonds worth Rs 5,000 crore have a bullet repayment in November 2026, while bonds worth Rs 1,100 crore have a bullet repayment in February 2028. In addition, GAL had raised Rs 400 crore via NCBs in April 2025, which have a bullet
<<PARA:3:40>> repayment in April 2028. This exposes the company to significant refinancing risk. However, a strong track record of timely refinancing mitigates this risk to an extent.
<<PARA:3:41>> Pledge of shares in GAL by the promoters, albeit decreasing, remains high: As of March 21, 2025, the promoters have pledged 35% of the GMR group's stake in GAL (down from 54% as of July 25, 2024) to secure debt at the promoter entity level. Any increase in pledged shares will be a key monitorable.
<<PARA:3:42>> Susceptibility to project risk arising from greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram and Crete and brownfield expansion
<<PARA:3:43>> at Nagpur: With greenfield airports at Bhogapuram, Andhra Pradesh and Crete, Greece under implementation, GAL remains exposed to project risk. Furthermore, the Airports Authority of India ('Crisil AAA/Stable') has earmarked 11 airports to be privatised in fiscal 2026. Winning the bid to operate, manage and develop any of these airports will also expose GAL to project related risk. Crisil Ratings has factored in equity support/investment of Rs 300-400 crore per annum towards these projects in the medium term. Any material increase in equity support will be a key sensitivity factor.
<<PARA:3:44>> Liquidity: Adequate
<<PARA:3:45>> The company had cash and cash equivalents of around Rs 340 crore against total debt of Rs 6,248 crore (excluding FCCBs and accrued interest) as on March 31, 2025. While the company had an interest obligation of Rs 962 crore in fiscal 2025, it resorted to cash coupon payments of Rs 387 crore for servicing its interest and balance through the accumulated interest. It has fulfilled its entire equity commitment in its operating airport projects, held via subsidiaries and JVs. The company is likely to infuse Rs 113 crore towards the Bhogapuram airport in fiscal 2026, of which Rs 51 crore has been infused till date.
<<PARA:3:46>> Environment, social and governance (ESG) profile
<<PARA:3:47>> Crisil Ratings believes the ESG profile of GAL supports its strong credit risk profile.
<<PARA:3:48>> · In line with the Airport Council International's (ACI) Airport Carbon Accreditation (ACA) programme, DIAL and GHIAL has successfully achieved Level 5 requirements, which is the highest-level accreditation of the programme. This makes GMR Airports the largest airport group globally to manage and operate Level 5 accredited airports. The airport at Mopa, in Goa, targets carbon neutrality and achieving ACI Level 3+ by 2027.
<<PARA:3:49>> · In 2024, airports under GAL increased its renewable energy consumption by 42% (year-on-year), with renewable energy accounting for 89% of its overall energy mix. This led to reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions intensity by nearly 72% (y-o-y) to 2.5 tCO2e per Rs crore of revenue reported. Both Delhi and Hyderabad airports operate on clean electricity, reflecting GAL's focus and commitment towards net zero emissions. This is achieved through a combination of onsite solar units and clean power agreements.
<<PARA:3:50>> . In fiscal 2024, women formed nearly 13% of total employees and the overall attrition was ~12%, at the consolidated level.
<<PARA:3:51>> · The governance structure is characterised by 50% of independent directors, ~6% women directors, a fully independent audit committee, largely independent risk management and nomination and remuneration committees, and extensive financial disclosures. The Board also has an ESG Committee which takes stock of ESG Progress on regular basis.
<<PARA:3:52>> Outlook: Stable
<<PARA:3:53>> Crisil Ratings believes GAL's business risk profile should strengthen, with the commencement of stable non-aeronautical revenue streams. The financial risk profile will improve, characterised by healthy cash accrual and deleveraging.
<<PARA:3:54>> Rating sensitivity factors
<<PARA:3:55>> Upward factors
<<PARA:3:56>> · Significant reduction in debt, leading to net debt/Ebitda (including dividends) of 5.5-6 times on a sustained basis, coupled with adequate debt servicing ability
<<PARA:3:57>> · Timely and healthy scale up of non-aero businesses, along with sustenance of a healthy operating margin
<<PARA:3:58>> Downward factors
<<PARA:3:59>> · Delayed correction in debt or lower-than-expected cash accrual from non-aero businesses, leading to net debt/ adjusted Ebitda of 9-9.5 times on a sustained basis
<<PARA:3:60>> · Depletion of liquidity, considering cash outflow via dividends, loans and advances, equity support to subsidiaries / SPVs resulting in stretched liquidity
<<PARA:3:61>> About the Company
<<PARA:3:62>> GAL is a leading airport developer and operator in India, with a portfolio of airports, including DIAL, GHIAL, GGIAL and Medan International Airport, as well as upcoming projects such as Bhogapuram International Airport and Crete International Airport (Greece), catering to millions of passengers annually. The company also recently signed the concession agreement for Babasaheb International Airports, Nagpur, further expanding its footprint in the country. The company has been promoted by the GMR Group, with a shareholding structure that includes Groupe ADP (32.3%), GMR group 33.8%), and other investors, showcasing a strong partnership between Indian and international stakeholders.
<<PARA:3:63>> About the Group
<<PARA:3:64>> The GMR group is a global infrastructure conglomerate with a diverse portfolio of businesses, including airports, energy, transportation, and urban infrastructure, operating in India, Asia, and Europe. Established in 1978, the group's business interests span multiple sectors, with a focus on infrastructure development and operations.

The Board of Directors also does not discuss any ratings at its meetings. 1 crore = 10 million Refer to Annexure for Details of Instruments & Bank Facilities Detailed Rationale Crisil Ratings has assigned its 'Crisil A+/Stable' rating to the Rs 6,000 crore non convertible debentures (NCDs) and 'Crisil A1' rating to the short-term bank facilities of GMR Airports Limited (GAL). The ratings reflect strengthening of the business risk profile of GAL, following the expected commencement of duty-free operations at Delhi International Airport Ltd. (DIAL; rated 'Crisil AA-/Stable') and GMR Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (GHIAL; rated 'Crisil AA+/Stable') in July 2025 and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. GAL already operates the duty-free business, car parking, and cargo handling for GMR Goa International Airport Ltd (GGIAL, rated 'Crisil PPMLD A-/Negative') and car parking and retail concessions at GHIAL. Additionally, GAL has signed a concession agreement to operate duty-free, car parking, cargo, and retail concessions at GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Ltd (GVIAL) at Bhogapuram, which is likely to commence operations before December 2026. These are long-term concessions concurrent with the tenure of the airport concession itself. Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards.

They will provide steady cash flow to GAL over a longer, given their monopolistic positions as exclusive operators in their respective airports, long term contracts for running these non-aero businesses, alongside a favourable outlook for air passenger traffic at these airports. GAL also has a proven track record of successfully operating these businesses through joint ventures (JVs). The ratings also factor in benefits available to GAL through its strategic co-promoter - Groupe ADP, healthy financial flexibility derived from being a listed holding company of two major operating Indian airports, DIAL and GHIAL, and demonstrated track record of having raised funds in the past to meet refinancing or capital expenditure (capex) requirement. The ratings remain constrained by elevated debt levels, exposure to refinancing risk in view of bullet repayments, and project risk associated with greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram, Crete (Greece) and the brownfield expansion at Nagpur. Analytical Approach Crisil Ratings has evaluated GAL on a standalone basis, factoring in support and equity commitments towards its subsidiaries/special-purpose vehicles (SPVs). Foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs) worth Rs 2,396 crore and optionally convertible and redeemable preference shares (OCRPS) worth Rs 260.4 crore to Groupe ADP, have been treated as neither debt nor equity. Key Rating Drivers & Detailed Description Strengths: Significant improvement in cash flow driven by non-aero business, aided by strategic location, exclusivity agreements, and long-term concessions, positive passenger growth outlook and seasoned management: GAL will benefit from its experienced management, favourable locations that it operates in, the exclusivity agreement and long concession period, along with a positive outlook on passenger traffic growth. Non-aero businesses are projected to form substantial part of total revenue from fiscals 2026 onwards.

Growth will be driven by commencement of duty-free operations at DIAL and GHIAL in July and August 2025, respectively, for a period of 10 years (extendable by 30 years) and 20 years, respectively. In fiscal 2025, the Delhi duty free and Hyderabad duty free clocked a revenue of Rs 2,200 crore and Rs 372 crore, respectively. GAL will now operate these concessions on sole basis. Demand-related risk is low, given the monopolistic nature of businesses and GAL's sole operator status at these airports, which would ensure stable cash flow for the long term. Expansion of retail and commercial facilities, enhanced passenger amenities, and improvement in overall airport experience, should aid in increasing the average non- aero spend per passenger. Hence, growth in passenger traffic and non-aero revenue per passenger will boost the operating revenue for GAL. Steady dividends from GHIAL and DIAL (expected in medium term), should further boost operating performance. Extensive experience of GAL's strategic co-promoter, Groupe ADP: Currently, the GMR group holds 33.8% equity stake in GAL, while Groupe ADP holds a 32.3% equity stake, with both entities having an equal board representation. Groupe ADP also has representation on the board of directors of all operational airports and key subsidiaries. As per the agreement between GMR and Groupe ADP, the GMR group will retain management control over GAL, provided it maintains a minimum 10% stake in the company. As a co-promoter, Groupe ADP plays an active role in shaping GAL's strategic and financial decisions, exercising oversight. Groupe ADP manages 26 airports worldwide, including three international airports in Paris. It is majority-owned by the Government of France with a 50.6% stake. Financial flexibility derived from direct ownership of airport assets: GAL, the parent company of DIAL and GHIAL, two major airports, benefits from their robust business risk profiles.

Revenue streams at these airports are secured through a hybrid tariff system, guaranteeing returns on aero assets. Passenger traffic at these airports, which accounted for about 30% of total air traffic in fiscal 2025, is likely to grow further. DIAL may also see its financial performance improve from fiscal 2026, driven by a significant tariff hike, pertaining to the completed capex. With this, dividends from DIAL are likely to flow in medium term. Post capex completion, GHIAL is also seeing growth in passenger traffic and revenue and is well-positioned to maintain this momentum. Steady dividends are expected to be accrued from GHIAL. Performance of GGIAL was impacted by subdued passenger traffic growth in Goa in fiscal 2025. Going forward, the airport's ability to ramp up passenger traffic and execute its real estate monetisation plans within the proposed timeline will remain a key monitorable. Proven track record for fund-raising: GAL raised Rs 5,000 crore via non-convertible bonds in the third and fourth quarter of fiscal 2024, prior to its merger with the erstwhile GMR Airport Infrastructure Ltd, to finance its existing debt, buy out 11% stake held by Malaysia Airports Holdings Berhad (MAHB) in GHIAL, and to maintain additional liquidity for equity investments in new projects. GAL has a proven history of securing funds to meet its refinancing and capex needs for its airport assets. Although successful fundraising has enabled the company to meet its refinancing requirement, high cost of debt had exerted pressure on cash flow earlier. Nevertheless, in recent years, the company has seen its cost of debt decline, which should have a positive impact on its financial performance. De-linking from GPUIL with no further recourse to GAL: As on date, GAL has no corporate guarantees or contingent liabilities related to GMR Power & Urban Infra Ltd (GPUIL).

The management has articulated that GAL will not extend any corporate guarantees or loans to any non-airport related business in future. That said, GAL has extended around Rs 2200 crore via inter-corporate deposits (ICDs; excluding around Rs 600 crore of accrued interest) to GPUIL and its subsidiaries. As per the management, GPUIL is expected to repay the ICDs between fiscals 2026 and 2029, which in turn will reduce GAL's debt and strengthen its financial position. Weaknesses: Elevated debt levels & refinancing risk: The company reported an elevated net debt (excluding FCCBs and accrued interest) to Ebitda (including dividends) ratio of 9.5 times as on March 31, 2025. As articulated by the management, the ratio is expected to decrease significantly over the next 3-4 years, driven by healthy cash accrual, which will be retained to reduce debt. Extent of deleveraging remains a key monitorable. The management has stated that GAL will start making dividend payments to its shareholders once it achieves its debt reduction target. Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) should remain comfortable over the medium term, supported by bullet payments and accumulated interest components of debt. Furthermore, the company's strong track record in refinancing and healthy valuations of its underlying assets will mitigate refinancing risk and offer some degree of comfort to manage the debt obligations. The GMR group intends to buy and convert FCCBs worth Rs 2,396 crore issued to Groupe ADP, over a period of time, without imposing any additional financial liability on GAL.GAL held NCBs worth Rs 6,100 crore as on March 31, 2025. Of these, bonds worth Rs 5,000 crore have a bullet repayment in November 2026, while bonds worth Rs 1,100 crore have a bullet repayment in February 2028. In addition, GAL had raised Rs 400 crore via NCBs in April 2025, which have a bullet repayment in April 2028. This exposes the company to significant refinancing risk.

However, a strong track record of timely refinancing mitigates this risk to an extent. Pledge of shares in GAL by the promoters, albeit decreasing, remains high: As of March 21, 2025, the promoters have pledged 35% of the GMR group's stake in GAL (down from 54% as of July 25, 2024) to secure debt at the promoter entity level. Any increase in pledged shares will be a key monitorable. Susceptibility to project risk arising from greenfield expansion at Bhogapuram and Crete and brownfield expansion at Nagpur: With greenfield airports at Bhogapuram, Andhra Pradesh and Crete, Greece under implementation, GAL remains exposed to project risk. Furthermore, the Airports Authority of India ('Crisil AAA/Stable') has earmarked 11 airports to be privatised in fiscal 2026. Winning the bid to operate, manage and develop any of these airports will also expose GAL to project related risk. Crisil Ratings has factored in equity support/investment of Rs 300-400 crore per annum towards these projects in the medium term. Any material increase in equity support will be a key sensitivity factor. Liquidity: Adequate The company had cash and cash equivalents of around Rs 340 crore against total debt of Rs 6,248 crore (excluding FCCBs and accrued interest) as on March 31, 2025. While the company had an interest obligation of Rs 962 crore in fiscal 2025, it resorted to cash coupon payments of Rs 387 crore for servicing its interest and balance through the accumulated interest. It has fulfilled its entire equity commitment in its operating airport projects, held via subsidiaries and JVs. The company is likely to infuse Rs 113 crore towards the Bhogapuram airport in fiscal 2026, of which Rs 51 crore has been infused till date. Environment, social and governance (ESG) profile Crisil Ratings believes the ESG profile of GAL supports its strong credit risk profile.

· In line with the Airport Council International's (ACI) Airport Carbon Accreditation (ACA) programme, DIAL and GHIAL has successfully achieved Level 5 requirements, which is the highest-level accreditation of the programme. This makes GMR Airports the largest airport group globally to manage and operate Level 5 accredited airports. The airport at Mopa, in Goa, targets carbon neutrality and achieving ACI Level 3+ by 2027. · In 2024, airports under GAL increased its renewable energy consumption by 42% (year-on-year), with renewable energy accounting for 89% of its overall energy mix. This led to reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions intensity by nearly 72% (y-o-y) to 2.5 tCO2e per Rs crore of revenue reported. Both Delhi and Hyderabad airports operate on clean electricity, reflecting GAL's focus and commitment towards net zero emissions. This is achieved through a combination of onsite solar units and clean power agreements. . In fiscal 2024, women formed nearly 13% of total employees and the overall attrition was ~12%, at the consolidated level. · The governance structure is characterised by 50% of independent directors, ~6% women directors, a fully independent audit committee, largely independent risk management and nomination and remuneration committees, and extensive financial disclosures. The Board also has an ESG Committee which takes stock of ESG Progress on regular basis. Outlook: Stable Crisil Ratings believes GAL's business risk profile should strengthen, with the commencement of stable non-aeronautical revenue streams. The financial risk profile will improve, characterised by healthy cash accrual and deleveraging.

Rating sensitivity factors Upward factors · Significant reduction in debt, leading to net debt/Ebitda (including dividends) of 5.5-6 times on a sustained basis, coupled with adequate debt servicing ability · Timely and healthy scale up of non-aero businesses, along with sustenance of a healthy operating margin Downward factors · Delayed correction in debt or lower-than-expected cash accrual from non-aero businesses, leading to net debt/ adjusted Ebitda of 9-9.5 times on a sustained basis · Depletion of liquidity, considering cash outflow via dividends, loans and advances, equity support to subsidiaries / SPVs resulting in stretched liquidity About the Company GAL is a leading airport developer and operator in India, with a portfolio of airports, including DIAL, GHIAL, GGIAL and Medan International Airport, as well as upcoming projects such as Bhogapuram International Airport and Crete International Airport (Greece), catering to millions of passengers annually. The company also recently signed the concession agreement for Babasaheb International Airports, Nagpur, further expanding its footprint in the country. The company has been promoted by the GMR Group, with a shareholding structure that includes Groupe ADP (32.3%), GMR group 33.8%), and other investors, showcasing a strong partnership between Indian and international stakeholders. About the Group The GMR group is a global infrastructure conglomerate with a diverse portfolio of businesses, including airports, energy, transportation, and urban infrastructure, operating in India, Asia, and Europe. Established in 1978, the group's business interests span multiple sectors, with a focus on infrastructure development and operations.
